housing.title: 1. Approved
paragraphs: A housing voucher helps pay the rent. A local agency pays part to the landlord; the household pays its share.
Approval starts a new task: finding a home where that help can be used.

housing.title: 2. Now find somewhere to use it
paragraphs: Find a home. Agree with a landlord. Complete the paperwork.
The agency checks the home and rent before the lease and assistance arrangements are completed.
Three parties must coordinate before the search deadline. Extensions depend on the local agency.

sources.label: HUD: searching, tenancy approval, and extensions

housing.title: 3. The doors that stay closed
paragraphs: A listing is not always an open door.
In this five-location study, voucher denial ranged from 15% to 78%. Scroll to compare the doors that closed.
These historical acceptance tests measure one barrier—not completed leases or current local rules.

sources.label: Urban Institute: five-site landlord acceptance study, published 2018

housing.title: 4. From voucher to lease
paragraphs: Follow 100 new voucher searches.
About 57 recorded a lease within one year in 2022. About 43 did not record that outcome.
The exact lease-up estimate fell from 65.7% in 2020 to 57.3% in 2022. These records show the gap, not every reason behind it.

sources.label: Furman Center: sample and one-year success rates, pages 8–10

housing.title: 5. Help with the search
paragraphs: What if the voucher came with practical search support?
In a Seattle–King County trial, 15% of the control group moved to high-upward-mobility neighborhoods. With a bundle of support, 53% did.
This measures neighborhood choice—not the overall chance of finding any home.

sources.label: Opportunity Insights: Creating Moves to Opportunity randomized trial

housing.title: 6. What counts as delivery?
paragraphs: The voucher is a commitment. The key is a usable benefit.
Measure what happens after approval: the search, the obstacles, and the lease.

medicaid.title: 1. Covered
paragraphs: Medicaid covers mental-health services. Coverage is the beginning of access.
This story follows adult psychiatric prescribing care: from a directory listing to an appointment offer.

medicaid.title: 2. Listed
paragraphs: Researchers sampled 80 listed clinicians in each of four cities: New York City, Los Angeles, Chicago, and Phoenix.
All were listed as accepting new patients in the city’s highest-enrollment Medicaid managed-care plan.
320 listings. The test was whether a call could secure an appointment.

medicaid.title: 3. Contacted
paragraphs: Start with the same 320 offices. Watch the listings separate into the outcomes of the calls.
57 offered the selected clinician. Another 30 offered an alternate. At 233 offices, no appointment was obtained.
87 offers out of 320 calls: 27.2%. An offer is not a completed visit.

medicaid.title: 4. Waiting
paragraphs: An appointment offer brings another question: when?
In NYC, 36.3% of sampled offices offered an appointment with any clinician. The median recorded wait was 28 days.
This is one plan’s sample of adult psychiatric prescribing offices—not all NYC care. Waits were missing for 17 offers across the four cities.

sources.label: JAMA: wait times and missing observations (Figure 1)

medicaid.title: 5. Accountable
paragraphs: A useful directory should lead to reachable, available, timely care.
A separate federal review recommended improving Medicaid directory accuracy. That recommendation is not a measured improvement.
When the first office cannot help, who helps the patient find the next one?

sources.label: HHS inspector general: Medicaid directory-accuracy recommendation
